utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar. Good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Merci. All the accused are here. Prosecution today is just Mr. McCloskey on his own. From the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon and Mr. Haynes and Mr. Lazarevic. Yes. Good morning, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue with your testimony today. I'm doubtful whether we will finish or not, but anyway we are approaching the end of your testimony. Yes. Mr. Petrusic, I can't see you. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before I continue, I would like to make a correction and to go back to 28 -- 279 page in the transcript. There is a mistake there which obviously is the consequence of our overlapping. I suppose my questions were delivered fast and your answer even faster, so I would kindly ask you to bear that in mind in the future. On page 28279 of the transcript, my question was ordered as follows: "Who in the administration supplied you with the elements that would allow you to issue your orders?" I am absolutely certain, and I checked my notes, that I did not say that. My question was rather as follows, and I am repeating it and rephrasing it. Who was it in the administration for operations and training who supplied you with the elements to draft your orders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received elements for the orders from our order issuer, the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In case the commander was absent, who did you receive the elements from?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the person who the commander authorised to stand in for him in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you name the persons who stood in for the commander in his absence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be the commander's assistants by and large.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, does this also apply to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff is also the deputy of the commander of the Main Staff, and this primarily applies to him. But he -- if he was also absent, then it would be a person authorised by the commander from the circle of his assistants by and large.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: So if such a -- an order draft was given, what would the commander or the authorised person do?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a -- an order that was drafted would be read by the commander and signed by him, then the document would be stamped and then the document could be forwarded to the commands in the units to which the order referred.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: A document prepared in such a way, could the commander change anything in it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Please, General, sir, could you please hold on just a little.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If in the meantime he changed his opinion or if any of the wording in the order did not please him, he would change that and then the act had to be redrafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You talked about your everyday duties as the chief of department for operations, could you also tell us what the role of the chief of administration was, the chief of administration for operations and training in the part of the front line where the commander was also deployed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would not have any special role. If he was with the commander, the commander was the one who was in command in that area, who coordinated all the actions and performed all other tasks and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the chief of administration for operations and training, could he coordinate any work relative to that part of the front line?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that part of the front line, coordination as a function of the command would be in the hands of the commander, because the commander was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And if the chief of administration for operations and training is in his position in the staff, what was his role with -- in respect of that part of the front line?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of administration follows the developments across the front line, and I suppose that his attention is less focused on the area where the command -- the commander can be found and more on other areas. If at any point in time, the commander showed interest in any of the areas where he wasn't at the time, the chief of administration could then provide him with quality and reliable information about those areas. That's why he was more focused on such areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge about the role of the Main Staff in combat operations which are planned and carried out by the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff, i.e., the commander approves such operations, the staff follows them, and reports the Supreme Commander, thereof, by way of daily combat reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And these concrete daily combat reports for the Main Staff, who submits those?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commands, the airforce, the anti-aircraft defence, and the centre of military schools.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce D51015 [as interpreted]. 5D1015 in the document number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please comment upon this document that you can see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document issued by the Main Staff, and it was registered in the administration for training and operations. It was drafted on the 17th of November, 1994. It was sent to the Herzegovina Corps, Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the Drina Corps, and the 1st Guards Motorised Brigade. These are units engaged in the Krivaja 94 operation. Their forces are engaged in that operation. The body in charge of the planning of this operation was the Herzegovina Corps. By issuing this act, the commander says that the decision of the commander of the Herzegovina Corps for this operation has been approved and that they can proceed immediately to carry out the operation that has been approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would that be a customary procedure to approve any decisions made by the corps on the part of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the ways. There are also other ways and other methodologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We can see that this operation was approved by the commander. In the case of the commander's absence, who would be the one to approve this operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This operation could be approved by the Chief of Staff as deputy commander by establishment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And in the absence of the both of them, would there be anybody else who could approve such an operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. While I was in the Main Staff or in general terms, I don't know if a decision on operations was approved by anybody who was either not the Chief of Staff or the commander himself -- of the Main Staff. I suppose that this is due to the fact that the principle of interchangeability has to be taken into account because operations are not something that you plan every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the administration for operations and training, does it have any role to play in the process to approve the commander's decision to carry out an -- a corps operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If documents are submitted in time, then the administration for operation and training will look at all the orders, the completeness of all the orders, and the decision of the commander on the map. And we provide our possible objections to the quality of the documents that we have perused. And then we forward our comments to the Chief of Staff. The Chief of Staff will then forward that document to the commander for his approval or he will return the documents to the corps commander for -- for their inputs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you mention the Chief of Staff and the commander in your answer, are you referring to the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and the commander of the Main Staff of the army Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely so, this is who I meant, because that would fall turned scope of their powers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in performing your tasks and duties as the chief of the -- the department for operations, you would be familiar with the term "monitoring." Are you familiar with the term, just please answer "yes" or "no"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Would the chief of administration for operations and training of the Main Staff be involved in the monitoring of the operations carried out by the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- it is the commander in -- who commands the operation, i.e., the corps commander, who also monitors the corps's operations. You can monitor on the ground but not from the headquarters of the Main Staff. When in the Main Staff, we followed the developments based on the reports that we used to receive in the course of every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Court please produce 5D1215.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, take as much time as need to look at this document. When you're finished, I'm going to ask some explanations from you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Within the context of my previous questions regarding monitoring, could you please comment upon this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document by the Main Staff of the army. It was drafted and filed by the administration for training operations on the 7th of June 1995. It was sent to the Herzegovina Corps to the forward command post of the Herzegovina Corps in Kalinovik, the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, the forward command post of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in Trnovo, the logistics sector of the Main Staff, and the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. It is said in the preamble that: "In order to assist the commands of the Herzegovina Corps and the Sarajevo Romanija Corps in stopping the enemy offensive in the general area of Kalinovik and Trnovo, the commander hereby issues the follows order. "In the course of -- 7th of June, dispatch from the Main Staff Colonel Nedjeljko Trkulja (team leader) and Colonel Mihajlo Durdevic to the forward command post 1 of the Herzegovina in Kalinovik." And the order also defines the time until which they are supposed to stay. Under bullet point 3, he also provides them with a task --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you, General. I would like to go back to my previous question when we are talking about monitoring. Does this document speak about the order of the commander of the Main Staff. He is -- dispatches the aforementioned officers to provide monitoring over this part of the front line?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Allow me, General, sir, let's not overlap. Could you please answer along these lines?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. Is there a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That was a leading question, but the overlap kind of un-did it. So it's not worth it. I'll just bide my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My intention was simply to avoid the exercise of reading the entire document, but I believe that everybody present will be able to draw their own conclusions from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: After your return on the 17th of July, after your return to the Main Staff, that is, what information did you receive about the evacuation; i.e., about the situation in the Zepa front line?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information from the daily combat reports, the regular ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did there come a time in the course of those days when you learned that the civilian population was being evacuated from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall when this information arrived, but I think we did, yes. I think we did have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did this information come through the reports from that part of the battlefield?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said previously, we got our information from the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When you say that you, in the plural, had information, does that imply that General Miletic also had that kind of information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether he had any special knowledge or information which he did not convey to you and the others who were in the staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to have any kind of special knowledge, he would have had to be there. I don't know whether he did, but I think didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether General Miletic participated in any way in the negotiations concerning evacuation connected with Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify that it doesn't -- it's not clear whether he doesn't have information or he wasn't involved based on that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information as to whether General Miletic participated in the negotiations concerning Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you hear at a later stage that he participated in the negotiations concerning Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was in charge of the negotiations concerning Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but if you are referring to the Zepa area it might have been General Tolimir or the commander; the commander of the Main Staff that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection to speculation. The witness should know he shouldn't speculate, if that's what that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We agree with Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Petrusic. So you either rephrase your question or you move -- and he answered it in any case, or you move. Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, do you have any information regardless of who the participants were as to whether negotiations on the evacuation of Zepa were held there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that General Miletic, to the best of your knowledge, did not participate in those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, that's not what he said. He said he didn't have information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic. I think Mr. McCloskey is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's rephrase the question, please, even though he answered "yes" to your previous question.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have in e-court P186. In the Serbian and in the English version, could you please scroll down so we can see the signature part of the document. It's on page 2 in the English version. And now, please, take the English version back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, have you had a look at this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Could we see the heading as well, please? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the heading it says, "Main Staff," and this number here, 12 -- strictly confidential number 12/45. Do you know whose number that is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the sector for security and intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We have some addressees listed here: General Krstic, the command of the 1st Podrinje Brigade, and Rajko Pusic, Captain Pecanac, the IBK, and the 1st Krajina Corps. So the Eastern Bosnia Corps and the 1st Krajina Corps. Do you know why the 1st Krajina Corps is among the addressees?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is the 29th of July, 1995, and the commander and most of the assistants of the chief of the sector and administration were in the western part of the war theater; and this is being sent to the 1st Krajina Corps so that the commander of the Main Staff would be made aware of this because that's where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please scroll down so that we could see the third paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look at this paragraph. Read it silently to yourself, and then I will ask you to comment on it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This paragraph amounts to an order. It says, "Continue combat operations ..." and so on. And it's addressed to the Drina Corps, to General Krstic personally, and to the command post of the 1st Podrinje Light Infantry Brigade; and the other security organs listed here belonging to certain units. The signatory who signs his name as the chief is probably Major-General Zdravko Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Very well. We won't need this document anymore.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's authorised by the commander to issue orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court document 5D1281.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Before you reply, I would like to ask you whether you know where, on the 12th of August, where General Miletic was on that day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Main Staff, in Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the remainder of the command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the Chief of Staff, do you know where they were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the command was in the western part of the front, in the area of the 1st Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In relation to this document, can you tell us what this document is about?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 12th of August, at 11.47, someone delivered to someone a copy of a conversation between General Miletic of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR in Bosnia Herzegovina, General Nicolai. There was an interpreter mediating in their conversation. General Nicolai thanked General Miletic for the medical evacuation which had been successfully completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Looking at this document, did General Miletic have authorisation to issue decisions?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the conversation one can see that General Miletic was unable to reply to the request from the Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR. He says here: "You know what, I'll consult my superiors, and I'll let you know." So he will receive a decision from his superior on the specific issue that General Nicolai wants resolved.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the course of this morning, General, we spoke about monitoring of one's own forces. I'd like to ask you the following: The term "monitoring," is it something that is part of military terminology in relation to enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who carries out that sort of monitoring?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Monitoring over the hostile or enemy forces is carried out by the intelligence organs at all levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the administration for operations and training, or in the staff, did you receive information about the enemy forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We received that information from the intelligence administration because its an essential element of planning. And we also received it through the regular combat reports from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said that this was an essential element of planning, are you referring to combat activities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the planning of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who is in charge of planning combat activities?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander and the command organs are in charge of doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether in the planning of combat activities the operations organ plays a part?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The operation organ coordinates work on the planning, the work of the other organs and draws up the combat documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And when these combat documents have been drawn up, does he take them to the commander or the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic, please. Just rephrase your question, unless you want to contest the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how these combat documents are drawn up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The documents that we drew up in the operations organs in the administration and in the department, we delivered to the Chief of Staff for his perusal. He inspects the documents and then takes them to the commander for his approval and signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Have you completed your reply?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And does the operations organ participate in the planning of all the combat activities that the units of Republika Srpska carry out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The operations and training organs of the Main Staff plan operations at the strategic level, operations of a strategic significance; whereas, at the operative level, it's the corps commands that plan the activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what the strategic level is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those operations encompassing the entire army or the forces of two or more corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: We are now talking about the operations organ in the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. Does he have any influence on the planning of operations carried out by the corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, except for the overview I mentioned when orders and decisions are entered into a map and sent from the corps command to the commander for his verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A correction. My question referred to operations planned by the corps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we don't participate in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you aware that the Main Staff, while you were there, established various forward command posts? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why these forward command posts were established?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forward command posts are established at all levels of command with a view to gaining a better insight into -- and the more efficient influence on the course of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Your information, based on the reports arriving from Zepa from General Tolimir, according to this information, what was the size of those operations? Were they large scale, small scale --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, foundational and leading to a point. He's not established these reports, what reports? General Tolimir's involvement in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, which reports are you specifically referring to? Forget about the leading, because to me, he hadn't finished the question as yet. But for the time being I think we need that information. Yes; Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a couple of foundational questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Are you following, Mr. Petrusic? Do you know exactly what's being required of you? Okay. Then go ahead. Mr. Petrusic, this the column is really creating a problem. I don't know, I mean I could interrupt you for two minutes, perhaps you could move somewhere where I can have eye-to-eye contact with you which, to me, as an experienced judge is very important. As it is, I can't see you, I don't know what's happening. So if you could move near Ms. Nikolic, for example, where I can follow you better it would be much appreciated. All right. Perhaps we can continue now, as Judge Prost is suggesting, and we will do that in the break. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, did you receive combat reports from the Drina Corps in the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did these reports contain, inter alia, information on certain events in the Zepa war theater?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you also receive certain reports from General Tolimir from that part of the war theater?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Based on these reports, as the chief of the department for operations, could you conclude -- were you able to conclude what sort of the combat activities and of what intensity were being carried out in that part of the war theater?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that intensity was, meaning the intensity of operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the forces involved, go, it was not a large-scale operation. It was within the zone of the Drina Corps. There were no forces from other corps acting jointly with them except for one unit of the 65th Protection Regiment, just a part of that regiment, they were active in that area. But all the rest were Drina Corps forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In this situation, do you know why General Mladic was there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the right of the commander to decide where he will go and where he will be at any point in time, to follow what's going on and who he will send there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You said you also had occasion to see General Tolimir's report. My question is: Do you know why it was General Tolimir who was there in that part of the war theater?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably that area, as regards intelligence and security, was of interest. The command there, for this reason, engaged the General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your testimony, was General Tolimir then a person who, acting on orders from General Mladic, monitored the operation at Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: If you are talking about the right of the commander as to where he wanted to be, do you know based on what he estimated and assessed the situation and its significance for an area so as to be able to decide where he wanted to be?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be based on the information that he received from the command organs. He would then make his own assessment and decide where to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: I don't want to lead you, although I am going to talk about notorious facts. Who was your immediate superior commander?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic, the chief of administration for operations and training.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who was your second in command?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the Main Staff, Lieutenant-General Manojlo Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In performing your tasks and duties, did you have an occasion to report directly to the chief of staff, General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rarely. My communication with him went through General Miletic for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In those rare occasions, did you have an occasion to deliver some documents to him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about the relationship between General Milovanovic and -- or, rather, what was the attitude of General Milovanovic towards the documents that he received?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just, foundational, what documents, when, what they had to do with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether this arises out previous questions, but I have my doubts like you. So perhaps, Mr. Petrusic, could you be specific as which documents that you wish to refer the witness to or that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You've already spoken about General Mladic and General Milovanovic and preparing some combat documents for them. Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you take these combat documents to General Milovanovic for his approval?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were mostly daily combat reports and orders, information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What was his attitude towards the documents that you would bring him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first when I arrived and later he -- he's a stickler for detail. He would read all these documents. He would correct the wording. He would even correct grammatical mistakes in these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the Court to produce D5 [as interpreted], the first page in the English version and in the Serbian version it will be the last page. P5. The document number is P5.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you have the document in front of you on the screen. As you are looking at the Serbian version of this document, do you recognise the signature?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the signature of the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff, Lieutenant General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us something about the contents of this document.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an accompanying document which was enclosed with the document of the upcoming directions which was submitted to the command of the 1st Krajina Corps. A request is made for one copy of this accompanying document in order to confirm the receipt of the aforementioned directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: It says in this document that this is directive --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: -- number 7. Is it? So this is an accompanying document for Directive number 7?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the left-hand side you can see the initials "JK/SZ." Are you familiar with the initials "JK"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Krsto Djeric, colonel by rank. I believe that SZ stands for somebody whose family is Zekovic, but I can't remember his first name. I've forgotten. The first set of initials represent the person who drafted the document, and the second set of initials represents the person who actually typed it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This accompanying document, together with the directive, was it submitted to General Mladic [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 21, page 15, instead of "General Mladic" it should read "General Milovanovic" -- line 14, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When this document reached him, did General Milovanovic familiarized himself with this directive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have been. He should have familiarized himself with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: As far as you were of his attitude towards documents that reached him, did he read this directive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given his position and duties that he discharged as well as the significance of the directive, as a general document issued by the highest of commands, a document that should have been applied over a long period of time, he must have read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: According to the best of your knowledge and military knowledge that you have about the drafting of a document of this nature, did General Milovanovic have to be privy to a document of this sort?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he had to be privy, especially in light of the fact that he was in the zone of the 1st and the 2nd Krajina Corps where he should have applied this directive, or at least he was supposed to apply it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Does it arise from this document that this Directive number 7 was sent to this corps, precisely there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in principle what the nature of a directive is, what kind of a document is that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A directive is a document used by high-ranking commands. It's a general act. It doesn't provide any details of any tasks, but it provides and outlines of the goals that a corps has to be aware of in order to issue orders to its subordinated units. And these goals are relative to the planned operations. In other words, there is no detail provided as, for example, in orders issued to the lower-ranking units.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us furthermore in principle, who are the persons involved in the drafting of a directive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The drafting of a directive involves the work of all the organs of a command.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now move on to the last page of the directive in both versions, in the Serbian as well as in the English version of the document. I'm looking for the last page until the English version and in the Serbian version it is page 11. In the Serbian version, it is 21. The last page in the English version. Yes, very well. In the Serbian version the page is correct, but can it please be scrolled up, page 21. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you can see here the term, "Drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic." Could you please interpret the term "drafted by" for us; what does the term mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The term "drafted by" means that the person unified all the elements received from other commands and merging those into a single document, i.e., this person received elements from all the organs that participating in the drafting of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: A document merged in this way or unified in this way, could you tell us what happens to it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the procedure, such a document is then submitted to the commander who was in charge of its drafting, who was responsible for the drafting; and that person is supposed to sign this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: This directive was submitted for signature to the Supreme Commander, then President Dr. Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could Dr. Karadzic change anything in this directive, i.e., the submitted document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His rights and powers allowed him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Let me be completely sure. You said that his right and powers allowed him to change the document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was the Supreme Commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about the chief of administration for operations and training, did he determine the contents of a directive in any way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of administration for operations and training did not determine the contents of a directive. The contents of a directive are defined by the competent organs and they provide elements. What they propose is accepted by the commander, and this is what is incorporate in a directive as far as the administration for training and operations is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you were in Crna Rijeka. Where exactly were you billeted during the discharge of your duties?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I had a room that I shared with another person which had a bed and a desk, but most of the time I spent in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what about General Miletic; where would he stay?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Miletic, he had his own room, but he also spent part of his time in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the extension 155?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Extension 155 was used by the Chief of Staff, but it was installed in two or three rooms; so it often happens in the operations room when the phone rang. I would pick up the phone and then General Milovanovic would tell me put the receiver down, because the same exchange was in the room where he spent his working hours as well as in the room where he rested.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who else would be in the operations room in addition to you and General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Krsto Djeric would be there and other organs of the staff would also come, the organs for various branchs. And when it came to the exchange of certain information and documents, some organs that did not belong to the staff would be involved in that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And what about the duty operations officers, where did they spend their time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had a special room in a special building below Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the so-called G1 facility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The underground facility?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When there was no imminent danger then we would be in the prefabricated facilities, and when there was danger they would force us to go up there to hide.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: What about this exchange 155, the telephone extension. Was this installed in the underground facility as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Up there was the main communications hub, the main communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will have a few more questions. I know it's not the time for our first break; however, if it does not interfere with your plans, I would kindly ask you to allow us to have our first break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's have the break now, but since I had an appointment, which now cannot be moved, the break will be of 30 minutes and not 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. -- I apologise. I will probably not have anymore questions, but I wanted still to have a consultation with my client. So pending that consultation, I may not have any questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem at all, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic, at least I can see you better now. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no more questions for the witness in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It will not be a problem with Ms. Nikolic because Ms. Nikolic I can see. So she is not behind a column. So let's do the round. Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No question for the witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please, go ahead. Cross-examination by Ostojic:

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: General Obradovic, my name is John Ostojic, and I represent Ljubisa Beara in this case. I would like to ask you a few questions, sir, if I may. Good morning, to you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Sir, in July of 1995, and I note that your first name is Ljubomir, were you known by any nicknames by either your family or your colleagues in the military?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My colleagues from the military usually addressed me as Obrad; in my family they call me Ljubo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did anyone in the military in 1995, July particularly, refer to you as Ljubo, to the best of your recollection?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some people did, but most of them called me Obrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to your testimony of last week, the 14th of November, and particularly just for the record, it's on pages 28275, and you were describing for the Court when you were giving an answer to my learned friend, Mr. Petrusic, an example where - it's on line 10 - where you say: "The corps commander did not dare communicate bad news to the commander of the Main Staff." And then you go on and gave us what seems to be a firsthand account of a discussion you had in the presence of General Tolimir; and you proceed to say where he called Stevo Bogojevic and asked him whether the information that he had actually received was actually true. You go on the next page just for reference sir, on page 28276, lines 2 through 5, you state as follows: "The latter confirmed that, and when General Tolimir asked him to write a report he said, 'Well, I can't. My commander won't allow me to write a report of that sort. This is, for example, one way of information reaching superior officers.'" Can you, to the best of your recollection in describing the situation, tell us when this event occurred that you were referencing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This event occurred in October 1994, and I refer to it as a typical example of something unusual happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And can you just share with us again that Stevo Bogojevic, he was in the 1st Krajina corps; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And he was a security officer in the 1st Krajina Corps, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Who was the commander at that time who is restricting him from providing written reports to the Main Staff regarding certain situations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Krajina Corps was General Talic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: That's all the questions I have. Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Ostojic. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thanks, Ms. Nikolic. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I have a few questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Or general, that's how I should address you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic, I appear for General Gvero; and I will ask you a few questions about your testimony. General, you said during your examination-in-chief that you arrived in the Main Staff around the 17th of July 1995. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the date when I came back from sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I was actually referring to. Let's go back to July 1995 when you returned. There was a command post in Crna Rijeka of the Main Staff and a so-called auxiliary command post in Hans Pijesak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff was deployed in two locations, in Crna Rijeka and in Hans Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In July 1995, when you arrived in Crna Rijeka, you didn't see General Gvero there, did you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when answering my colleague's questions, the questions of Mr. Petrusic, you spoke about the way documents and directives of the Main Staff are drawn up. Do you draw a distinction between the documents drawn up in the Main Staff and the documents drawn up in the Supreme Command? There is a difference between those two types of documents, is there not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about the way in which these documents were drawn up, you were referring to the ones drawn up in the Main Staff were you not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Directive number 7, to be specific, that you were asked about, was issued by the Supreme Command, was it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the one we saw was signed by the president of the republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, who was the commander-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the title -- in the heading, it says, "Directive of the Supreme Command," does it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your explanation as to the manner how directive could be drawn up, was based on your knowledge and experience, but is theoretical is it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't there when any of these directives were being drawn up. I did not participate in drawing them up nor was I present when they were being drawn up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I was getting at. You arrived in the Main Staff in September 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The directive which was issued before Directive 7 was directive number 6, and that was issued in 1993. I assume you were unable to participate in its drafting?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you were absent from the Main Staff from January 1995 until July 1995 when Directive number 7 was be compiled, so you were not able to participate in its drafting either?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was absent from the 27th of January 1995 to the 17th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Directives numbers 8 and 9 were drawn up in forward command post 1 and Drvar respectively; so you were not able to participate in the drafting of these either, were you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I will move on to another topic. When you were referring to the organs of the Main Staff, you mentioned a term which has to do with the corps. You spoke about command. According to the practice and the documents of the army of Republika Srpska, the corps had commands and the Main Staff was the Main Staff. And there was also the Supreme Command at Pale. Do you draw a distinction among these terms?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Staff was the command, because it had the commander of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska and the chief of staff of the Main Staff of Republika Srpska. I do not deny the existence of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But the term usually employed was Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about -- well, according to my information, there was a collegium in the Main Staff, a narrow collegium and an extended collegium. Do you agree that the term used was "collegium"?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the narrow part of the command, the collegium, is comprised of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat the answer, the last part of the answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, the interpreters didn't catch the last part of your answer. If you could repeat it, please. Well, I will read out to you what we have in the transcript so far. The question was: "Do you agree that the term used was 'collegium'"? And you answered: "Well, the narrow part of the command, the collegium is comprised of ..." that's where we need you to continue, from there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a synonym. The collegium and the narrow part of the command are synonymous. They refer to one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the collegium would be what is comprised of what or whom, so that we make sure that we are on the same wavelength.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's comprised of, Your Honours, the commander and the assistant commanders and the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to a topic we had mentioned previously. When you arrived in July 1995 in the Serbian language, you told me you did not see General Gvero at all, but it's not reflected in the transcript. So could you repeat your answer?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 17th of July on my return from sick leave, I did not see General Gvero on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And later on in the course of July, although you mentioned this, the Main Staff went west; but you didn't see General Gvero in Crna Rijeka, did you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I said they went west, all the assistants went there, the Chief of Staff and the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: There is another point I wanted to clarify with you, Mr. Obradovic. When you spoke about the right of the commander, or, rather, the absence of the commander, and how the Main Staff functions in his absence, you said that according to the establishment in the absence of the commander, he is replaced by the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The command post of the Main Staff was in the zone of responsibility of the Drina Corps, was it not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when the commander was in the area of the Drina Corps, there was no reason for him to be replaced by anyone because he was in constant communication with the Main Staff, was he not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander, wherever he is on the territory of Republika Srpska, has communications with the Main Staff and the subordinate units. But he was nearby in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when you spoke about the manner in which the Main Staff functions, you spoke on the basis of your experience and your professional knowledge?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, experience and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you never saw a written order where Mladic authorised someone to stand in for him in his absence or to deputize for him; and I'm referring to the time-period up to the point where we they have all went west?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any order signed by him personally, but I didn't need to see it. It wouldn't referred to me, so there would be no reason for me to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You are not aware in a General Gvero ever deputized for General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot assert that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you're not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said he was not aware of it but it's not reflected -- ah, now it's in the transcript; I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, it's the commander's right, at any point in time, to designate someone to carry out a certain QT or to entrust a certain function to someone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's his right. But there is a hierarchy to be observed. He's not going to designate me to deputize for him when he has close associates who are senior in rank and position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, Your Honour. Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Sarapa.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: No questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. The ball is in your court, Mr. McCloskey. You had asked for three hours; is that still your estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I hope it will be shorter than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, is there a possibility that we will send the gentleman back home today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let's proceed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So I take it General Gvero was a close associate of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, was his assistant for morale.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: With a long history of knowing each other and working together as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they had known each other for a long time, but they worked together from 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me first ask you, you were obviously a -- a serious officer as the chief of operations at the Main Staff in 1995. When you wrote a document and submitted it to your superior, General Miletic, did you take responsibility for that document, for its content, for its recommendations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My responsibility was to deal with a document professionally, but the responsibility lay with my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Meaning General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and his superior was also responsible for him because whoever signs a document has to read it. If he trusts his subordinate, he might do it without inspecting the document first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So documents containing suggestions, goals, analysis, that came out of the operations branch in the name of General Miletic, General Miletic would take responsibility for that information as it went up the line to his superior?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and his superior was duty-bound to control him or to monitor him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, just talk briefly about directives. We see that Directive 7 came out of the operations branch. Before getting to President Karadzic, did it -- did it go from its drafter, Miletic, to Milovanovic or should it have gone to Milovanovic if he was around?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A directive is compiled based on certain assessments of the relevant officer, the commander issuing it. There must have been a discussion in a certain circle for General Miletic to be given the task of drawing this up; and if his immediate superior was there, he would show it to him, for him to check it and give suggestions, and then to give him the green light to go to the commander who has to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we know Directive 7 wasn't signed by Mladic, but if -- let's just say for hierarchy's sake that Mladic, Milovanovic, the assistant commanders, and the operations people, Miletic, got together, had long meetings about what was going into this, perhaps they had some input from the president's office; but then it gets drafted. Let's say it goes to Milovanovic, then Milovanovic would send it to General Mladic, wouldn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you be one moment, before you answer I see two Defence counsel to on their -- Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that this question calls for speculation by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That was going to be our objection, in particular in light of the answers the witness gave to Mr. Krgovic's questions; namely, he wasn't there at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey. Thank you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the basic procedure of following a document is something that this witness can testify. He testified at length in his direct examination about these sorts of issues. This is nothing very mysterious nor I don't think very controversial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, the question does pose a hypothetical case, and it's not based on an event that is alleged to have taken place. Still, we believe that it would only call for speculation if the witness doesn't know how to answer and he just provides us with a guess. But if he knows the answer to such a question in such a hypothetical case, then he should answer the question. So we only want you to answer the question, Mr. Obradovic, if you can give us an answer based on your experience in the VRS army and your knowledge of how things proceeded during those times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, we can start over again. It's probably easier. The document comes out of the operations group. It should go from Miletic to Milovanovic if he's around, General Mladic probably wants to see it as well, correct, before it goes to Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the directive was drafted on the 8th of March. I've just seen it. I did not participate in the drafting of this document. However, the tasks and the conclusions that were passed towards the end of January, after the analysis of the combat readiness of the army Republika Srpska, which involved the participation of the Main Staff, which means the commander, his assistants, corps commanders, the Supreme Commander and his organs. This analysis gave rise to certain conclusions which were the basis for the drafting of the directive that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. General, I am just trying to get a -- what should be the normal path of this directive before it gets finally signed off by Karadzic. So if Milovanovic is there, you say he's a stickler for detail, he wants to see it. Would Mladic want to seen it as well if he was there before it goes to the president, or would he see it under the rules that you were living by?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to procedure, General Miletic should have shown the proposal of the directive to the commander, if the Chief of Staff was not there, before sending it off to Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And if the Chief of Staff was there, and he showed it to the Chief of Staff, would it still be seen by Mladic in your view under the way the procedures -- and you know General Mladic better than we do.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to procedure, the Chief of Staff would be duty-bound to show it to General Mladic of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then it would go to the president's office in Pale, I take it.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you know who -- who would first see it in Pale, a document of this import coming out of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not entirely sure. Maybe it would be the Minister of Defence or maybe it would go directly to the president. I am not aware of the methodology of the receipt of documents over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Fair enough. And I think you've said of course that the president, President Karadzic could take his pen to the directive and write in what he wanted to, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was his rights to reformulate, rephrase, add something, eliminate other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure, but after he did that, if he did, it would go back to the Main Staff for the final typing, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And at that point General Miletic would certainly see any changes that President Karadzic had made, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but was not allowed to change anything, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Certainly. How about would General Mladic want to look at it or would General Mladic see it as well when it comes back from the president's office, if it's not signed when it comes back and it's got changes in it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just out of curiosity but there was no reason for him to look at it. He will receive this document in its final form, anyway. Once it was sent to the president, the president signed it, and the document will end up with the commander of the Main Staff for his information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as you said, the Main Staff assistant commanders all played a role in putting -- making their input in this document - and we can see that in the various headings of the document - so I take it the assistant commanders would also be able to see this directive after it was completed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous question that you put to me, it's beside the point to send it again to the Main Staff commander because he no longer had a say in it; whereas, during negotiation he did have a say in it. That's why he would eventually receive this document as the final document for his information and perusal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Understood. But my question was would the assistant commanders that played such a role in providing information for this document, would they see this document before it was signed off on by the president? Would these the draft?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they participated in the drafting, then yes. And maybe they would ask for it out of curiosity, but I can't really give you the exact procedure. I don't know what happened with this particular one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. Now you have told us that General Miletic, or Colonel Miletic for a time, was receiving the very important information from the corps in the form of daily and interim combat reports. He was getting phone calls from the 65th Protection Regiment in the morning and in the evening. You told us that the corps commanders would call and speak to Mladic in the evening, and when that happened would important information that Mladic received through the corps commanders be passed on to General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, when General Miletic receives this information, let's say especially when he receives an interim combat report from a corps where there is serious things going on, people's lives are being lost. He doesn't merely just pass on information to his commander, does he? He reviews this information, he studies it, and he analyses it; and he sends that information on to his commander that is the result of his study and his experience as a general, officer, or as a colonel, depending; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He passes on information. If combat operations call for a brief review and his position on the course of the combat operations, he may give his assessment; however, if he receives information, he has to pass it on in its authentic form to the commander. He must not reshape this information in any way, he must not tamper with it in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Of course. But he has the bigger picture than the commander does because he's received information from various corps from is a lot more information than the commander has had time to take up, so in many cases the commander want to hear his evaluation and his analysis and his identification of problems, doesn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the information, problems identified by the subordinate commands, each with its respective zone was responsibility. I am talking about corps commanders. A summary of those identified problems was sent to General Miletic. Since our operations centre was not organised as it should have been, then the administration for operations and training received this information, merged this information, and informed the Chief of Staff; and the Chief of Staff would then pass it further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But the commander would want Miletic's evaluation on how to solve those problems, wouldn't he? Especially if Milovanovic wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At his specific request, he will certainly have his position as an officer and will be able to meet the commander's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In other words, the request to provide insight, analysis, recommendations, and proposals. That's his job in part, isn't it, to provide those things to the commander or the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: For example, an operation may be in great need of fuel. We know fuel was a very tight commodity. Information could come up through the corps to General Miletic that fuel was a big problem, and it would be General Miletic's job to try to sort out how to get the fuel to where it needed to go. Of course, looking to his superior's, Milovanovic and General Mladic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Any requests for material and technical equipment would go along the line of logistics support, and logistic organs of the corps would then request from the operations logistics organ to supply them with certain things. And replenishment is done based on daily consumption, losses, and approved quantities that the commander approved either by issuing a directive or an order, as well as based on certain norms of expenditure. In their daily combat reports, corps commands would also add their requests in addition to what they had already written to the logistics sector of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, I am not speaking of sort of normal situation. What I am meaning to refer to is the situation, first of all, in Potocari when there was thousands of Muslims that needed to be shipped out of the area and fuel was in a difficult state. Now, if General Milovanovic isn't at the HQ, he's off in the Krajina, and the Drina Corps needs fuel, who is to coordinate with the logistics branch and to get that fuel or to figure out a way to get that fuel if it's not General Miletic, chief of operations and training, who is standing in, in part for General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the basic activity of supply with fuels is not what operations organs do. It is what logistics operations organs do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But when General Miletic -- when General Milovanovic is not there, you've already acknowledged that General Miletic is doing many of the daily tasks that General Milovanovic would normally deal with. Clearly, your not suggesting Milovanovic from the western front is -- he's got his own problems with fuel, he wouldn't be the one that's sort out fuel for a Drina Corps operation right near Hans Pijesak. It would be Miletic who is if one that's doing lots of his daily tasks, wouldn't it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you answer or -- go ahead, answer the question. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, supply with material technical equipment, and fuel is a basic activity of the logistics operations organs in the logistics sector. And this resupply is based on daily consumption, losses, approval quantities, the quantities that were approved by either director -- directive or an order by the commander and norms applied in such case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Earlier on, before you started giving your answer, I noticed General Miletic wishing to communicate with his counsel. Do you still wish to communicate with your counsel, Mr. Miletic? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. McCloskey, you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
