utterances.text: General, on the subject of nicknames, you've told us yours. We've heard the name Toso before, can you tell us who had that nickname, if anyone?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it was General Tolimir's nickname. I believe that that's what he was called for short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you -- I've got translated "I suppose." But you're pretty clear, you know that that's his nickname, right, back in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't call him that. He is my senior, those who could did. Yes, they did call him Toso for short.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how about General Miletic? What did people sometimes call him as a nickname?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico would be the customary shortened named of all Milovanovic, Miletic, and people bearing similar family names. Mico would be the shortened version of those.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, my question wasn't what would be in the former Yugoslavia the nicknames. I was asking specifically. We've seen the name Mile referring, I believe, to General Miletic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have foundation for this claim, please -- this assertion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, what's the foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My good faith belief, and the presence of it on intercepts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We don't have a problem with the question, please. So let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, have you heard General Miletic referred to as Mile?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico, not Mile. Mico.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'd like to go over some documents with you. The first one I want to go over with is Directive 6, which was mentioned by one of the Defence teams. It's also mentioned in Directive 7 which was dealt with as well, and it was mentioned that it -- well, and we'll -- if we could see it briefly. Let me give a hard copy so you can take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 3919.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just a few questions about this. If we -- it's dated 11 November, 1993, sent to all the corps. It's -- like Directive 7, it's under the name of Radovan Karadzic, and also like Directive 7, you can see at the end it's drafted by Colonel Radivoje Miletic. So just a couple of things I wanted to ask you, because it's referred to in Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we could go, it's page 3 in the English, it should be under paragraph 2(c), under prospects on the Serbian version. But these are just short snippets, and I am not asking you to evaluate this whole thing. It's a big, strategic, clearly well-thought out major document. And it's page 3 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's talking about battles with the Muslims and the HVO, and it says: "In further battles, the use of chemical agents, irritants, can be expected. The production of more dangerous chemical agents, which may be used at critical moments, can be expected in the next four to six months." Can you tell us what is meant by the chemical agent irritants, is that basically tear gas?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this is chemical agent that the normally used by the units of the military police, tear gas as you've called it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It also says that: "The production of more dangerous chemical agents which may be used at critical moments." Surely your aware of the more serious chemical agents that the JNA had in production. What is this referred to, what kind of dangerous chemical agent are they referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer the question, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am just somewhat confused. Can we see first of all to which army this is referring to? I think this is somewhat problematic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I said it in the question. It's their word that the Muslims and the Croats had this stuff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's clear enough, Ms. Fauveau. In any case, if the witness has problems in understanding the question, he may ask for a clarification and I'm sure Mr. McCloskey will comply. Judge Kwon is drawing my attention that the witness said something that does not show in the transcript, so I think we need to do -- take care of the first. I am going to read to you, Mr. Obradovic, what we have in the transcript. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No there is no discrepancy. It's still not clear in my mind. We are talking about combat operations with the Muslims and the HVO, but who, in fact, was taking part in combat operations between the Muslims and HVO, were there Serbs involved as well? This is what I would like to know, I find it problematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey, do you wish to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As I mentioned, it's not my intention to get into the details of -- of this, except to clearly point out like I did that we are not talking about the Serbs having this stuff. It's what they are concerned the Muslims are having.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that answers your question, Ms. Fauveau. We still have got something missing from the question. Mr. McCloskey, the last part of which, if you look at lines 23 and 24 of the previous -- of page 46, we have: "What is this referred to? What kind of dangerous chemical agents are they referring to?" And then there is something missing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think I just cut I myself off. Sometimes I do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Anyway, perhaps you can repeat the question at this point to the witness who must have lost track, and he can answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, we know, and you know, that there is one of the branches or organs is chemical, biological, and something else, I can't remember right now, warfare, and clearly you, as an experienced officer, can tell us what this more serious irritant that is referred to in this document drafted by General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not found this formulation in my copy. You say it's 2(c). This concerns information about the enemy, about the armed forces of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, and these are assessments provided by the intelligence organ. But based on what information this assessment was made, that the enemy has -- have these means at their disposal, I don't know; and I don't know what means precisely are being referred to. I only know what I learned in theory about protection from chemical, nuclear, and biological weapons; but what precisely is referred to here in this case, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm glad they never dropped any on you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to your next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you want to say something, General?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to add that this part of the directive was drawn up by the intelligence organ, the administration for intelligence affairs, which is in the security and intelligence sector. General Miletic put all that together in this document; however, the content belongs to the intelligence officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, keep looking, go to number 3. It's called, "The Task of the Army of Republika Srpska." Which branch or unit would have drawn up this section?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But was one of the Main Staff branches? Is this operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part of the tasks of the army is drawn up in the staff. The proposal for the use of their own forces is done by the operations and training organ, but also the organs of the various branches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. This -- this directive, Directive 6 and Directive 7 are stored at the Main Staff and available to you and others at the staff that want to review it, I take it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the date of this directive, it's the end of 1993, and I arrived in the second half of 1994. So I didn't use it. I didn't find it necessary in order to actually see it. It was not at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But you were able to review and see Directive 7 and Directive 7.1 while you were at work in 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, Directive 7 you may not recall makes a reference to Directive 6, but let's -- I don't recall exactly where it refers us to Directive 6; but just briefly, if we can look under this task of the army of Republika Srpska, the second paragraph. It talks about: "During offensive operations, regroup the main forces ..." and then there is a loft discussion about improving operational position, shorten the front line. And then number three, it says: "To create objective conditions for achievement of the strategic war goals of the army of Republic including ..." and then it lists --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It lists several war goals. Were you aware of the strategic objectives of the VRS? Do you know what they are talking about here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. One moment, sorry, sorry. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was not familiar with these strategic goals. I was not aware of their existence in this directive because I didn't actually have the directive in my hands. Now, I see four goals listed here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, sir, we have seen significant documents in this case where the -- there is a reference to the six strategic objectives, something that was signed off by Mr. Krajisnik in 1992. Have you ever heard of the six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when the indictment against Mr. Krajisnik was published, because the people around me asked me about this event; and I would often say how can an army be successful if it doesn't have any goals, any goals in combat. But didn't know about these goals before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Now, I would like you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would like to go to, we are under paragraph number 5. It's page 5 in the English. And it's under the Eastern Bosnia Corps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. General Miletic, what's the problem? THE ACCUSED MILETIC: [Interpretation] May have two minutes to consult with my counsel, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, of course. Ms. Fauveau, if you wish to speak to him outside of the room -- it's okay. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, we can proceed. Sorry for you interrupting you like this, Mr. McCloskey. You were, lines 7 to 9 of page 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. There is a --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just looking at the section regarding the Eastern Bosnia Corps, I don't want to read the whole thing, but as we get to about line 5, 4 and 5, it's talking about launching operations to destroy the enemy forces around certain villages, roll them back towards Tuzla and Srebrenik, other things, and within coordination with the Drina Corps and the first KK, launch fierce attacks to crush the Ustasha forces on the northern and eastern slopes of Mount Majevica. Now, the forces they are talking about on the slopes of Mount Majevica, the enemy forces. What does Ustasha refer to, is that Muslims forces or Croat force or both, or neither?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it would be most suitable if it referred to the Croatian forces, because that was the term used to refer to the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, I think we all know that based on World War II. Are those Croatian forces that they're talking about there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are mostly Muslim forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, looking at the Drina Corps, it's the next one down. It says: "Use some of the forces to maintain the blockade of enemy forces in Zepa, Srebrenica, and Gorazde enclaves, and constantly inflict [Realtime transcript read in error, "conflicting"] losses on them and disrupt their communications." Now, the date of this, November 1993, its page 5 in the B/C/S, what does that mean? I mean, this is a -- there is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Finish your question, and then we hear Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We think everyone will agree that there are protected enclaves at that point, and I understand what "block them" means; and we know they had enemy forces inside those enclaves. But what I would like you to explain is why would you then be constantly inflicting losses on them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be an idea if the witness took off his earphones, assuming he doesn't speak English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think I did ask him the question last Friday, and Mr. Obradovic said he doesn't understand English. So could you kindly remove your headphones, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have already objected to this line on the basis the witness was not involved in the preparation of this document. But perhaps we could make a further objection and really invite the Prosecution, through Your Honours, to say where this is going and why they say this particular witness is competent to answer these question, how it arises from the examinations hitherto, although, I accept of course this cross-examination; but really where this is going and why this is an appropriate witness to ask about this particular document. Which, hitherto, as far as I am aware, hasn't been introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Josse. I am sure that you would like to comment to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. First of all, I think they brought up Directive 6, not me. It's amazing to me that these kinds of arguments are made when they bring them up. But, more importantly, I -- because I don't think they brought it up very [indiscernible] frankly, but they did. I think it's pretty clear to me that the point -- well, I think the Court knows the Prosecution's position on Directive 7 and the two paragraphs in it. One to make life miserable for the Muslims, to make life impossible to be there; and then create a situation of permits that restricts aid but doesn't make us look terrible in the international community. Those are two bad para-phrases of the critical points in Directive 7. Now, I believe the direct examination of the witness was designed to suggest that he merely was drafting it and that perhaps these bad sections were added by somebody else and that he is not in the know and is not part of Directive 7 and not a big player in Directive 7. I think that's what's coming. I think that's what we've seen on direct examination. So -- but you now know that Directive 6 was drafted by Miletic. So he is an experienced draftsman in this area; and I think the material, especially as it regards to the Drina Corps and the history as it relates to the enclaves, is very important assist getting into his mind as he is the drafter of Directive 7, a document that has been historically incredibly important for this case and for the Trial Chambers and for the Appellant Chambers that have reviewed it. So the door is wide open on directives and the man's drafting of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, one moment. Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I briefly deal with the Gvero position on this. Mr. Krgovic cross-examined on Directive 6 on an extremely limited basis, as my learned friend has just conceded; namely, to illustrate that the witness wasn't present in the Main Staff when that was drafted nor Directive 7. Nothing else. Now, the rest of the response of my learned friend relates primarily to General Miletic and the questions asked by Mr. Petrusic on his behalf, and it's perhaps therefore -- it doesn't fall to me to answer those points as such. But, Your Honour, if it's suggested that by our cross-examination of this witness on Directive 6, that's opened the door to this line, then we refute that and invite the Court to say that simply isn't right and proper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse, but I think that there is more to it than that. Our rules provide limits and extensions to those limits when it comes to cross-examination, and provided there is relevance to anything that is an issue, we cannot stop the Prosecution from putting such questions. But in any case I need to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we are unanimous again on this. It's a perfectly legitimate question which the witness should be able to answer. I think the -- you can either summarise it again or put the question again, Mr. McCloskey; or I do it for you, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'll try one more time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, getting back to where we were on the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you are looking for your -- the text of your question, you need to go first to lines 11 to 14 of page 52, and then lines 19 to 22; and I point out to you that the last line contains a mistake. It's not -- it shouldn't be constant conflicting losses but constant inflicting losses and you can take it up from there. It's an easy question which can be put again to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, the question is, everyone understands that this was the so-called protected enclave and, well, in particular Srebrenica; and we understand that you would -- that there were significant enemy forces in Srebrenica at the time and that they needed to be blocked, and their communications disrupted. But can you tell me what is this reference to constantly inflict losses on them. Why is that a goal, a strategic goal, for an enclave where the -- we don't have active military operations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the enclaves, there are constant incursions with small sabotage groups, there were ambushes on the roads, civilians were killed and houses set on fire. For these reasons, it says here that such activities should be prevented, activities of members of the army of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if that's so, keep looking down the paragraph because then it's talking about Gorazde. It says: "Group your forces as you see fit. And with the appropriate re-enforcements, improve your operational position in the Sarajevo area in keeping with the approved decision." And then this is what I want you to concentrate on: "Use some of your forces to coordinate actions with the Drina and Herzegovina Corps in crushing the Muslim forces in the Gorazde area." And then next paragraph it also says: "Use part of the force to crush and destroy the Ustasha forces in the Gorazde area in coordination with the Drina Corps." This seems like a lot more than just hitting the Muslim forces and crushing them when they come out to wreak havoc. It is, isn't it. It's more operational to keep them under military pressure?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, before you answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like the witness to take his headphones off please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Could you take off your headphones, please. Thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a little bit confused, I wanted the Prosecutor to let us know, does he mean holding the Serbian forces of the opposing side under pressure? Is that the position of the Prosecutor during wartime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam Fauveau. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: My question was suggesting to him that this indication is much more than just a prevention and a strike back at the Muslim forces. That is an operational objective of offensive nature to put pressure on them militarily by -- as described in this document, as opposed to what he said earlier that this is just fighting with the guys that come out and the wreak havoc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Do you wish to comment further, Ms. Fauveau or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I still have the same problem. Why is it a problem to hold these people under pressure, the Muslims forces. The problem may relate to the population. But here we are talking about the forces, I don't see why this is an issue. I real don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can point to specific evidence in the indictment that makes it an issue, if you want to hear it. The names of the victim that died under this kind of conduct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We see no problem with the question, and we also wish to point out that ultimately it's us that will need to decide what weight to give to this consideration or opinion of the Prosecution. So let's proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, the question was: Isn't this language about using your forces to destroy the Ustasha forces in the Gorazde area and crushing the Muslim forces in the Gorazde area; doesn't that mean what it says, crush the Muslims forces in the Gorazde area and get rid of the Gorazde enclave?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not my interpretation. You said a little while ago that these were so-called protected areas because we had large forces of the army of BH in these areas. It's as if there had been parachutes dropped behind the lines of the army of Republika Srpska, because every day they were wreaking havoc; and they were a legitimate target of the army of Republika Srpska. I am referring to their forces which were in Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, General, I am not sure that I would disagree with you on that point. And this is whether or not the attack on Gorazde -- or a potential attack on Gorazde, excuse me, or the Srebrenica attack on Gorazde, was military -- militarily justifiable, is not something I want to get into with you. What -- all I am asking you is Gorazde was a real thorn in the side of the VRS, they had forces in there, and the VRS wanted to take it out and get rid of it, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wouldn't have been a problem had there been no armed forces in Gorazde, but they were at division levels, and they were engaged in combat against the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I agree with you, and therefore it was the aim of the VRS to go in there and crush those -- that army and get that army out of there, to stop them from -- from doing that, defeat them completely militarily.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any way conflict, the aim is to defeat the opponent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And there is nothing wrong with that, I'm just saying that that's what this is saying, let's defeat the Gorazde opponent, let's go in there and crush them militarily, completely. Correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be a conflict with the enemy forces. I don't see any problem there. If someone is inflicting losses on you every day, making normal life impossible, attacking civilians, burning houses, they have to be prevented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We are not making a subjective judgment, we are just trying to determine what this says. So this says go in and clear out the enemy and defeat them, correct? In Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What passage is that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: "Use part of the forces to crush and destroy the Ustasha forces in the Gorazde area in coordination with the Drina Corps."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, part of the forces to keep.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the paragraph above that: "Use some of your forces to coordinate action with the Drina Corps and the Herzegovina Corps in crushing the Muslim forces in the Gorazde area."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the passage starting with the Drina Corps, there is no statement of that sort, defeat finally. It says to keep them in the enclaves of Zepa, Gorazde, and Srebrenica. To inflict losses, and to disrupt their communication and put up decisive defence on the front towards Kladanj and Olovo. There is a constant threat coming from Kladanj and Olovo. Actually, the threat is that the forces from Kladanj and Olovo would link up with the forces in the enclaves, and that was a constant threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We talked about that in Srebrenica, I am now talking at the bottom here, Gorazde. There is no discussion like there is about Srebrenica. Gorazde, all Gorazde says is crush and destroy the Ustasha forces. And all I'm asking you is doesn't that mean defeat them militarily?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in this case the Ustasha forces are the Muslims forces?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who drafted this or typed this, I really don't know why he put "Ustasha" there. I suppose that the reason was the fact that the Ustasha forces in the second World War had a lot of Muslims as their members. I don't see any other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You don't think it's because all sides in war come up with really derogatory nasty names to call each other? We are not here because of nasty names, General; but isn't this what is about? This is just a nasty name being used in a document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As by the same token as they called us Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's break time. 25 minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, General, let's go to Directive 7 now for a little while, hopefully not too long. I think you told us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Oh, it's 65 ter number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think you've told us you did have a chance to look at that because it had more application for your time-period when you got there in July; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at 7/1, but then I saw this one as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you saw 7/1 but you also saw Directive 7, this one that we have in front of us now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And by seeing it did you review it, you know, back in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When did you see it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of August, September, of the same year, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did -- how was it that you happened to review it in August or September 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in General Miletic's strong box.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What else did he have in his strong box?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A pile of papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, we won't explore his strong box this afternoon. Why did you go to his strong box to get the directive?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He ordered me to find some other document. I came across the directive, and I had a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you read the whole thing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at the information about the enemy and the tasks of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's -- if you could, it's -- should be page 8 in the English, page, I think it should be 11, but it's pretty much -- it's number 4 where it says: "I hereby decide ..." And just looking at the paragraph right above number 4, I just -- and I not -- I don't really want to go into this in detail, but we can see that there is a comment that it says: "And thus, by force of arms, impose the final outcome of the war on the enemy, forcing the world into the recognizing the actual situation on the ground and ending the war." So is it fair to say that at the time this was written, the -- there was actually a belief that the war may end, that the planning for the end of war is actually happening?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we see number 4 -- sorry, number little (4) in that same paragraph, it's the last line of below that part about ending the war, it says: "To create optimum conditions for the state and political leadership, to negotiate a peace agreement, and accomplish the strategic objectives of the war."

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, this is -- is this the same strategic objectives we saw in Directive 6?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be sure, but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with the goals. It's impossible for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's just go to -- it's number 5, it's "Unit assignments." That's the one you are interested in, right, it should be just below the part that you are looking at. It should --

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that the one that you looked at that you said you were interested in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who would have put that -- put that part together, the unit assignment section, 13 in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer this question, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection -- it is not an objection, Your Honour, but the relevant page is not on the screen, so we kindly ask for the page to be put on the screen. So this is not an objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Fair comment. Can you help us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I just said 13, maybe it didn't get translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is 13; 13 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Maybe 11. It's 13 -- no, Ms. Stewart is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's page 13, Mr. Petrusic. All right. Okay, I think having -- I think I understand with Mr. Petrusic to be okay, and we can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So which branch put together this unit assignment section?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that it was the organ for operations and training and arms organs that do that. They put proposals for the use of their own units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So General Miletic would have played a role in this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go -- it should be the next page in English, page 9. It's really the second -- there is just another reference to the Ustasha forces, which I won't go into. So don't worry about that. Now, it's page 10 of the English under the Drina Corps section. It's after the East Bosnian Corps, you probably know the order. I believe it's page 15 of the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- B/C/S. I don't -- I won't read this out again. We've heard this quite a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Have you read the Drina Corps section part about making life for the inhabitants of Srebrenica unbearable? Okay, I think that speaks for itself. What I wanted to ask you about is the sentence that starts: "In case the UNPROFOR forces leave Zepa and Srebrenica, the Drina Corps command shall plan an operation named Jadar with the task of breaking up and destroying the Muslim forces in these enclaves and definitively and definitely liberating the Drina Valley region." So is it fair to conclude at the time that this was drafted there weren't any plans to really take on the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa until the UN forces left?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, if we could go over to page 12 in the English, it should be page 17 in the B/C/S. Just a small point under the Herzegovina Corps section where they are talking about specific plans, and the naming of specific plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says, in the 7th paragraph down from what I'm reading, that: "By the end of March 1995, the Herzegovina Corps command shall plan operations for reaching the Neretva river valley named Krivaja 95 and for coming out on to the coast ..." and it goes on. Now, who was responsible for naming these operations? In this case it looks like clearly the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, we all know, and I think that you do, that the name of the operation to separate the Zepa and Srebrenica enclaves and reduce them to urban areas was named Krivaja 95. So do you know who would switched the names from this Herzegovina Corps title to actually giving this Krivaja 95 on to the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer your question. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But it would have to be somebody in the Main Staff, I would think.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. The document may be signed only by the person who -- the document may be altered by the person who signed it, and the signatory of the document is the Supreme Commander, Karadzic. A subordinate officer is not allowed to alter anything in his superior's documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if General Zivanovic as he was, in his staff at the Drina Corps, were beginning the operations and the planning - and I should say General Krstic as well - in let's say June, they couldn't just pick Krivaja 95 without getting Main Staff approval, could they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The approval of the person who signed the directive in the first place. This is the person that they should ask approval from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, the Drina Corps wouldn't go directly to the president's office, would they, in that request? Wouldn't they follow the chain of command, put their request through; or maybe they are getting it fed down to them from the Main Staff. I understand you weren't there at that time period but ...

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should not have been the case. However, I remember that on television President Karadzic, and I will paraphrase his words, it impossible to quote him. He said he had issued an order to General Krstic who had planned the whole thing, and he commended him for good planning of the whole thing. That's more or less how I heard it on television. And according to the rules of subordination, they should not skip one person in the chain. They should not go one step above without the knowledge of their immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if General Miletic is involved in drafting and sorting out these different names for the operations which must be crucial important, General Miletic should have been involved in the changing of the names whether it be Karadzic or General Miletic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, there is no foundation for this question. The Prosecutor only assumes, speculates, without providing any foundation. So far the witness has not told us anything to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's just a question based on all of his testimony and logic that if General Miletic is and the operations unit has drafted this part; and obviously we can see made very careful consideration about names, that when a name change occurs on a plan involving the corps that the drafter of those names would be involved somehow in the name change so that it could be distributed throughout the Main Staff and other corps so there would be no confusion. That's the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- if he can't answer, he can't answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We agree 100 per cent with your reasoning, Mr. McCloskey. Let's revert back to you, Mr. Obradovic. If you can answer the question, please, go ahead and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this may also be a sign of a lack of discipline and unfairness of the corps command towards their first immediate superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's go on. Do you know lieutenant-colonel -- at the time Lieutenant-Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic? He was commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him only when he arrived in the command of the East Bosnian Corps. This may have been even after the war, I don't know when exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He was a career JNA officer, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what he looks like. I know him personally, but I believe that I met him in the command of the East Bosnian Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I don't know when this was. I believe that it was after the war as I've said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know at what rank he retired, assuming he's retired?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was a colonel when he retired, if we are talking about Slavko Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay, I ask you because in on the 14th of July he made a report, it's 65 ter number 3177, basically to the members -- to report to his brigade members. And he made a comment to them remarkably similar to the comment that we saw in Directive 7. He said: "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible so that they leave the enclave, en mass, as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." So aside from what I just read to you and what you read in Directive 7, have you heard this idea, this goal, this thought, in these very particular terms? Have you heard of it, and at your stay in the Main Staff or in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just a coincidence?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not wish to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I'll withdraw that. I'm sorry, I shouldn't ask that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to 65 ter 3043. This is Directive 7.1. So let's trade again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we recall, this is something that you said you did -- you did read. Is that the one that you read in August or September when you looked at Directive 7; or did you look at it before? And yes, take your time to look at it if ... so is this the one that you've had the chance to see for the first time in August or September 1995 like you've said before?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we see that this is dated on the 31st of March, 1995. Directive 7 is dated 8 March 1995. And if we go to the end of this we see that this is also drafted by Miletic, but now we have the commander, Ratko Mladic signing off on this one. Okay. Just a couple of things I want to check with you. So let's go to the second page in the English and the second page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just the last line of kind of the -- what is the first numbered paragraph. It says, as it describes a whole lot of brigades, basically, talking about the Muslim units, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says: "Other details of the intentions and possibilities of the enemy forces are in Directive number 7, and the daily intelligence reports of the VRS Main Staff." So is it fair to say that when Miletic was assembling this, drafting this, that he must have clearly read and known what was in the signed version of Directive 7 when he was drafting this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in fact, under this "Tasks" part of it, the first line is on the basis of the Directive number 7, the VRS has the task. And so it cites Directive 7 and then it gives more task and more particularity, isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the original document is Directive number 7 of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And let's go to page 4 in the English, it should be page 3 in the B/C/S. It's under number 4, but it's one of the last big paragraphs before you get to number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And it says: "Other forces of the VRS shall contribute to the conduct of Operation Sadejstvo 95 with the goal of operative strategic camouflage and correcting the operative tactical position by carrying out planned combat, battles and operations in accordance with Directive 7. And active combat operations towards Bugojno, Travnik, Kladanj, Olovo, and Vares, and around the Srebrenica, Zepa and Gorazde enclaves and the Bihac Pocket." So now we have this saying that combat operations should happen around the Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde enclaves. What do you think that means? And it's citing in accordance with Directive 7.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It implies that at a certain moment, and it says the moment is withdrawal of UNPROFOR, to -- for operations towards the enclaves to be planned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do you see a reference to the withdrawal of UNPROFOR in this document, or are you just taking it from Directive 7?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Directive 7 where it actually says so. In this document no references made to the UNPROFOR withdrawal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. That's your interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to the next page, 5, in English; and it looks like it should be B/C/S 5 as well. And it's paragraph 5.3, and we're at the Drina Corps section.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says -- well, I won't read the whole thing. Well, I might as well: "The Drina Corps: Prevent an enemy break through along selected operative tactical axes with persistent defence and active combat actions on the northwest part of the front and around the enclaves, and tie down as many enemy troops as possible through diversionary actions and operative tactical camouflage measures." Okay, we've talked about a similar reference, so I don't want to go into most of this. I just want to ask you about this term, "Diversionary actions." That means sabotage action, doesn't it? Going into the enclave and conducting sabotage.

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is no reference to sabotage here. Shall I read it back to you, will you allow me to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me ask you, I've heard the 10th Sabotage Detachment referred to as the 10th Diversionary Detachment, and I've heard the words used interchangeably. So that's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you answer the question, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there is a mistake in the translation. I would like the witness to read this in B/C/S and make sure we can check the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objection to that? I suppose not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, he's got it front of him. I think that's important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need to know, too. Especially if there is an alleged error in translation; we know we have need to know if that's correct and where it is. Which is on the screen we have the English and the French -- and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's a diversionary action I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think the witness can understand what the Prosecutor is saying. I think it's important that the witness reads 5.3 in B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- so that everything is clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we have 5.3 in B/C/S in front of us. I would assume that the witness has it too. We could actually have just the B/C/S on the screen, and we zoom in that part of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, its just the last line, basically. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Last line of which of those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The last line of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the comma, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Perhaps the witness can read it out aloud and we can have a translation of it or interpretation of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it says here: "Demonstrative actions and application of measures of operative and tactical masking to tie up as much of its force." So the word is "demonstrative" not diversionary, so this is not a real attack but just to demonstrate in order to tie up as much of their force. It is not a diversion but a demonstration. And also operative and tactical masking measures are ordered in order to cover up the real intention so as to leave the enemy with an impression that an attack would follow soon, so this is the intent of the measures of operative and tactical masking and demonstrating force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yet we might have had a translation problem there, General. But let me ask you what I was getting to. Surely you've heard of the famous incursion by the 10th Sabotage Detachment through the tunnel into the Srebrenica enclave in early 1995?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the detail of those activities, but I know. I have heard of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I am sure you have given its a Main Staff asset, but have you heard of their operation when they went into the enclave through that tunnel?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not privy to the details. I know that there was the 10th Sabotage Detachment which was tied to the intelligence administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you say you're not privy to the details, but have you heard anything about the 10th Sabotage going into the enclave in 1995 before the Srebrenica operation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to page 7 in the English, page 7 in the B/C/S, just a quick question about something in the engineering support section of this important document. And it's the -- 6.4 is the number of the paragraph where the engineering support is. And the last line of that second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It says: "The VRS Main Staff will approve mines and explosives for erection of obstacles and for demolition in response to specific demands and availability." So did the -- this is correct, I take it, the Main Staff actually watched very carefully and wanted -- or required -- excuse me, required approval before people used explosives for the demolition in response to specific demands and availability? So explosives for demolition were a very carefully controlled item by the Main Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first paragraph here, under 6.4 speaks about the focus of engineering support, and that should be to safeguard the movement of the units. And the second important thing is to fortify the achieved lines. Also, a references is made to particular attention to be paid to opening pass through our own obstacles and so on and so forth. And as for what you have asked me, it says here that the Main Staff will approve explosive -- explosives for these -- for the engineering support. The personal tactically in charge is the head of engineers in the Main Staff of the -- of the Main Staff of the VRS. He's the one who worded this bullet point 6.4 about the engineering support of combat activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. But it means what it says, the Main Staff has to approve demolition materials in response to various -- or specific demands? It means what it says, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Sir, it's the position of the Prosecution that there became a -- a real demand for demolition material, probably right around the time you got there on 17 July, because somebody - maybe you can tell me - blew up every mosque that was in Srebrenica, and dropping a minaret, so it hits the dome takes a lot of skill if its done right. Same thing happened in Zepa; it took a lot of demolition equipment. Clearly, with major operations to blow up these big buildings, the operations branch would have known about it, correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person in charge and the person who is the one recording all the mines and explosives is the chief of engineers of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. What were the tasks underlying the request for demolition materials and explosives, I don't know; I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, you are not going to put the blowing up of the mosques on the chief of engineers, are you? Is that what you're saying, he's the one responsible for this?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not blaming anybody. I am not putting down responsibility on anybody. I am just telling you what I know. We are talking about bullet point 6.4 which was defined and provided to the administration for operations and training the chief of engineers. That's who did it. As for mines and explosives and demolition materials, these are all things that are operatively monitored by the chief of engineers. The decision as to what facility will be blown up and when is not his. I didn't -- I never said that he was the one who said to blow up things, but this is within his purview, and the resupply of the explosives and demolition materials is his call upon requests received from subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you have any information whatsoever who was involved in the operations to blow up the mosques of Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: LJUBO OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You haven't finished. How much more do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: One second, Mr. President. Let me take a look at my binder. I will need another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So, as I expected, Mr. Obradovic we haven't finished. We will continue tomorrow. And same advisory as last time. Please don't discuss the subject matter of your testimony with anyone between now and tomorrow morning, at 9.00 when we are to reconvene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1.46 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of November, 2008, at 9 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
